# The Easy Way to Stop

> "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
>
> — 1 John 1:9

This is the chapter with the instructions in it. Follow them and you'll find stopping somewhere between easy and enjoyable. There are only two:

1. **Decide that you are finished with lust: the porn, the hand and the chase. Never again.**
2. **Don't mope about it. Rejoice.**

The Bible has older names for both. The first is *repentance*. The word doesn't mean feeling dreadful. It means a change of mind: you turn around and walk the other way. The second is *receiving grace*. You're forgiven, so you act like a forgiven man.

Decide and rejoice, or repent and receive. That's the whole method.

The Introduction said to make no vows, and that still stands for the vow you used to make. That was a promise to go without something you still wanted. This decision is a different thing. It comes at the end, when you no longer want what you're leaving. That is why it holds.

"Then why nineteen chapters? Why didn't you say so on page one?"

Because you've done the first half before. You decided, with tears, more times than you can count. Then you moped, the moping turned to craving, and one gray evening you un-decided. The decision was never the hard part. Your decisions didn't stick because you still believed you were giving something up. That belief is the Big Monster, and it had to be dismantled lie by lie before these two lines could do their work. Once you know how the trap is built, walking out of it is simple.

## One man's last time {-}

Here is how it ends for a man who gets out this way. He has spent years on the other method: vows at retreats, on New Year's Day, on mornings when he couldn't look at himself. Then one day a different thought frightens him properly. *What if I simply do this for the rest of my life?* For once he stops vowing and starts watching. He asks what he is actually getting, and the honest answer is a few seconds of relief and then the familiar flatness. He talks to men who have quit, and expects to find them hanging on by their fingernails. Most of them laugh. "Miss it? You're joking." So he says to himself, out loud: "Like it or not, that was the last time." He expects months of climbing the walls. What he gets is relief on the first day, and it doesn't leave.

Why does that attempt go so smoothly? Because the terrible cravings he braced for don't exist. Doubt creates them. A man suffers only when he wants it and thinks he can't have it. Even in the trap you go whole days without it when you're busy or traveling, and you barely notice. The misery comes from the dithering, the "maybe just tonight", the door left ajar.

So the key is to make it certain and final. Don't hope you've stopped.

Know it.

But how can a man be certain at the very start? That is what the rest of the book is for.

## You're free the moment you decide {-}

When you make that decision, you're already a man who doesn't do it. You don't become one after ninety days or after the Little Monster dies. You become one in that moment. A recovery writer put the new identity in a single line: "Begin to say, I am a man (or woman) who does not use pornography, masturbate, or lust."

So don't sit about waiting for the itch to fade before you allow yourself to be happy. Get out and live right away.

This is where the Christian has an enormous advantage, if he'll take it. Look at the verse at the head of the chapter. Confess, and he is *faithful* to forgive. It doesn't say he might, or that he will once you've proved yourself with a decent streak. And then: "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1). The word is *now*, on day one, with the Little Monster still grumbling.

One man, who now teaches other men about this, spent years repenting and falling until he saw what was wrong with his repentance. It was all about him: how bad he was, how hard he'd try. "The foundation of my repentance was me", he says. Then he turned it around, and this is the sentence to carry out of this chapter: "Our motive for repentance is the fact that God is good. Not the fact that you are bad."

A pastor draws the same line between two kinds of sorrow. Worldly sorrow is sorry it got caught, and it defends itself and plays the thing down. Godly sorrow is sad to have grieved someone who loves you. Under that first man's story a listener wrote what the difference had done for him: "'Breaking God's heart' just changed my whole entire mindset." The first kind of sorrow leaves a man staring at himself, and the second gets him looking up. So be sorry for what this has cost the people you love. Then get up.

Remember from Chapter 1 that guilt loads the gun. The man who decides and then spends three weeks feeling filthy is moping in religious clothes, and it ends in the same place. Grace is what makes instruction two possible. You rejoice because the past really is dealt with. A man of forty-three, who had fasted and read his Bible over it for years, summed up his freedom in three words and capital letters: "JESUS DID IT!" That is what rejoicing sounds like, and you can start on the first day.

A psychiatrist has noticed what frightens the men he treats about stopping: "if I stop, I have to face the guilt of having screwed up the last 10 years of my life." That fear has an answer, and it's the one this chapter has been giving. The ten years are confessed and forgiven. You don't have to carry them, and you don't have to keep the habit going to avoid looking at them.

If you're not a believer, the same advice holds: drop the self-hatred. It never helped you once. Decide, and be glad.

## The thread pays off {-}

From the Introduction on, this book has said that **a man who can't control his lust can't be trusted.** Here is the other half.

You probably thought self-control meant what you'd been doing for years. You gripped the rail with white knuckles, a strong man holding down a strong desire. That's a wrestling match, and you know who usually won.

Real self-control is quieter. It belongs to a man whose mind is no longer divided. He isn't holding anything down, because there's nothing pushing up. Paul lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit, and you saw in Chapter 3 how fruit grows. Thomas Chalmers, a Scottish preacher of two hundred years ago, explained how a desire actually leaves a heart: "the only way to dispossess it of an old affection is by the expulsive power of a new one." Freedom is a new affection, and so is a clean conscience. Christ is the greatest one there is.

And here is the payoff. The moment you decide and mean it, you have given your word and you're going to keep it. For the first time in years you'll be a man who can believe his own promises. Trust starts there, and your wife, your friends and your work will feel it in time.

Fitness for service starts there too. A sober soldier doesn't spend his watch fighting the bottle. He has stopped wanting it, and he can be put on the wall.

## Two warnings {-}

**First: don't make your final decision until you finish the book.** I know. You're ready now. But the last step is in Chapter 27, and there's a little more to put in place first. Until then, carry on as normal, as Chapter 1 told you.

**Second: don't misread "the first weeks".** The next chapter says the Little Monster takes a few weeks to starve. That doesn't mean a few weeks of suffering. And it doesn't mean holding out until day twenty-one, because nothing magic happens on day twenty-one. A man who mopes for three weeks will be moping in the fourth.

You can't order yourself to feel glad about losing something you still think is valuable. Nobody can. That is why this book has spent nineteen chapters showing you that the thing is worthless. You aren't losing anything. Once you know that, the gladness comes by itself.
